quote: This person will never understand physics no matter how many books they read.
content: By this test, Feynman, Bohr and Einstein will never understand physics. Feynman: “I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics” (The Character of Physical Law, 1965). Bohr, as reported by Heisenberg: anyone not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it. Einstein called entanglement “spooky action at a distance” in a 1947 letter to Born. The people on record calling quantum mechanics weird are the people who built it, and the pattern is not accidental: the sense of strangeness is the sense that the ontology does not fit the concepts one has, and it is present in proportion to how seriously one takes the question of what the formalism describes. The attitude the essay prescribes, in which the amplitude cloud is “perfectly normal” and only the reader is weird, has a name in the field, “shut up and calculate,” and Mermin, who coined the phrase, has spent decades explaining that it was a complaint, not a recommendation. The essay is entitled to say that incredulity wastes emotional energy. It is not entitled to say that the physicists who felt it did not understand physics, since they were the ones who did.

quote: The universe was propagating complex amplitudes through configuration space for ten billion years before life ever emerged on Earth. Quantum physics is not “weird.” You are weird. You have the absolutely bizarre idea that reality ought to consist of little billiard balls bopping around, when in fact reality is a perfectly normal cloud of complex amplitude in configuration space.
content: This is wavefunction realism, the view that the fundamental thing is a field on 3N-dimensional configuration space and three-dimensional objects are derivative, and it is one position among several inside the Everett camp, let alone outside it. Wallace and Timpson argue for “spacetime state realism,” on which the fundamental ontology is assigned to regions of ordinary spacetime (Wallace & Timpson (2010)); Maudlin argues that a world that is “only wavefunction” cannot recover the three-dimensional world it is supposed to explain (Maudlin (2010)); Bohmians, collapse theorists and the pilot-wave school all say the amplitude cloud is not the whole story. The essay tells the reader to reshape their intuitions to conform to reality, and then identifies reality with one contested interpretation’s contested ontology, forty essays before the quantum sequence argues for it. The instruction to feel that configuration space is “normal” is an instruction to adopt a metaphysics; the essay presents it as an instruction to stop being stupid.

quote: Probability theory tells us that surprise is the measure of a poor hypothesis; if a model is consistently stupid—consistently hits on events the model assigns tiny probabilities—then it’s time to discard that model. A good model makes reality look normal, not weird
content: Two senses of surprise are run together. The surprisal of an outcome under a model, −log p, is what probability theory measures, and by that measure quantum mechanics surprises no one who uses it; its predictions are the best-confirmed in science. The “weirdness” the essay is scolding is not predictive surprise but conceptual: the formalism yields the right numbers while resisting every attempt to say what it is about, which is the measurement problem, and it is not a quantity in any probability distribution. A physicist who says nonlocality is strange is not reporting that Bell-test outcomes had low probability under their model; they are reporting that the model that predicts them has features (no joint distribution for the local variables, Bell (1964)) that no classical account can share. Calling that a symptom of a “viewpoint already proven erroneous” assumes the ontological question is closed, and the essay’s own book concedes in Many Worlds that the Born rule remains unexplained. An unexplained thing is a legitimate object of the word “weird”; the essay has confused the feeling that one’s model needs work with the feeling that reality is misbehaving, and the first feeling is the one physicists report.

quote: It shouldn’t be hard to imagine how a PhD physicist ends up believing in astrology. People compartmentalize, enough said.
content: Four essays earlier, in Outside the Laboratory, a scientist who compartmentalizes “literally doesn’t know why you have to look at things,” has only been trained in “a certain ritual of experimentation,” and cannot be trusted on open questions in their own field. Here compartmentalization is a normal feature of human psychology, and anyone who does not find it easy to imagine has a defective model of people. Both cannot be the book’s position. If compartmentalization is ordinary enough that failing to expect it is a modelling error, then the physicist who believes in astrology is behaving as human cognition predicts, and the alarm of the earlier essay was misplaced; if it is instead diagnostic of never having understood the method, then this paragraph’s “enough said” is a curiosity-stopper of the kind the book warns against. The transfer literature cited in the annotations on the earlier essay supports this essay’s version. The book keeps both, and uses whichever one the argument of the moment requires.
